Sagara, Bhagiratha and the Descent of Ganga

Stories from the Ramayana · Bala Kanda

Sagara, Bhagiratha and the Descent of Ganga

The Story of the Liberation of Sixty Thousand Sons

In everyday English — the tale of Bala Kanda, sargas 38–44

Stories by Eku

How to Read · · BEFORE WE BEGIN

Read it out loud. This story is made to be told. Read slowly, as if you were sitting with your family and telling it to them.

This book carries the story forward from the last one. On the banks of the Ganga, after hearing the story of Kartikeya, Rama asked — how did Ganga come down to earth? And Vishwamitra told this story — of King Sagara of Ayodhya, of his sixty thousand sons, and of Bhagiratha, whose penance brought Ganga down from heaven to earth.

The yellow boxes are the characters speaking in their own words. Change your voice a little when you read them — Vishwamitra's calm and deep, Sagara's royal, Garuda's gentle.

At the end of each part there is a green box — Pause and think. Stop there. Ask the question. Let the listeners speak. This story is about three generations of penance — and about a king who never gave up. Thinking about that is the real lesson of the book.

The main story of this book is from the Ramayana, Bala Kanda, sargas 38–44 — as Valmiki has Vishwamitra tell it. Where other tellings say something different — like the place of Bhagiratha's penance, or who Kapila was — that is given separately at the end, under Where This Story Comes From. Nothing has been mixed into the main story.

One part carries a ◆ mark — where the sixty thousand sons are burnt to ash. That part is not for younger listeners. It is told in plain words, without frightening detail.

Who's Who · · THE CHARACTERS

Vishwamitra — the great sage who is taking Rama and Lakshmana to Mithila. On the road, he is the one who tells this story. White beard, saffron robes, a calm and deep voice.

Rama — the young prince of Ayodhya. Tall, warm dark brown skin, black hair tied back, simple gold jewellery, a bow on his shoulder. In this book he is the listener — and the one who asks the questions.

Lakshmana — Rama's younger brother. He walks beside Rama and listens to the story with just as much attention.

Sagara — king of Ayodhya, of the Ikshvaku line. Two wives — Keshini and Sumati. He performed the horse sacrifice.

Keshini — Sagara's elder queen. Her son Asamanja — who was cruel, so Sagara banished him from the city.

Sumati — Sagara's younger queen. Her sixty thousand sons.

Amshuman — Asamanja's son, Sagara's grandson. He went to search for the horse and came back after seeing the heaps of ash.

Dilipa — Amshuman's son, Bhagiratha's father. He too did penance for Ganga, but did not succeed.

Bhagiratha — Dilipa's son. Through his penance Ganga came down to earth — which is why Ganga is called Bhagirathi.

Kapila — an ancient sage sitting in meditation in the nether world. Calm, grave, never shown in anger.

Garuda — Vishnu's eagle, Amshuman's maternal uncle. He told Amshuman that only Ganga's waters could liberate the sons.

Brahma — the creator, four-faced, in white robes. He gave Bhagiratha the boon.

Shiva — the moon in his matted locks, a snake and rudraksha beads around his neck, a tiger skin for a garment, a calm face. Only he could bear the force of Ganga.

Jahnu — the sage whose sacrifice ground Ganga flooded — and who drank Ganga up.

Ganga — Himavat's elder daughter, the river of heaven, now about to come down to earth. Fair, in a white-and-blue saree, adorned with water flowers.

Indra — the king of the gods. He had taken the sacrificial horse away.

1 · King Sagara of Ayodhya · · KING SAGARA OF AYODHYA

Morning came on the banks of the Ganga. After hearing the story of Kartikeya, another question rose in Rama's mind —

Rama asked: “Teacher, Ganga is the river of heaven — then how did she come down to earth? Tell me that story too.”

Vishwamitra said: “Listen, Rama — this story is from your own line. The story of King Sagara of Ayodhya.”

Long ago, in Ayodhya, there was a king named Sagara — of the Ikshvaku line, your own ancestor. He had two wives — Keshini and Sumati.

Keshini had one son — Asamanja. But Asamanja was cruel — he tormented people and caused them pain. Sagara banished him from the city.

Sumati had sixty thousand sons — all together, sons of one mother, all brave, all alike.

Sagara was a great king. He thought — I shall perform the Ashvamedha — the great horse sacrifice, in which a horse is set free, and wherever the horse goes, that land is counted as the king's.

Pause and think — Sagara had two kinds of sons — one cruel, who had to be banished from the city, and sixty thousand of whom he was proud. Can a father see his sons differently — punishment for one, love for the others?

2 · The Sacrificial Horse · · THE SACRIFICIAL HORSE

The sacrifice began. The horse was adorned, mantras were chanted, and the horse was set free — wherever it went, Sagara's kingdom would extend that far.

But where did the horse go? Indra — the king of the gods — took the horse away and hid it.

The sacrifice stopped. Without the horse the sacrifice could not be completed. Sagara called his sixty thousand sons and said —

Sagara said: “Sons, find the horse. Go below the earth, go above — wherever it is, search it out and bring it back.”

Sixty thousand sons set out — to find the horse.

Pause and think — The horse was lost — and the sacrifice stopped. Can one small theft stop a great sacrifice? And when a work comes to a halt, what should be done — give up, or keep searching?

3 · Sixty Thousand Sons Dig · · SIXTY THOUSAND SONS DIG

The sixty thousand sons searched the whole earth. They went above, they went below — but the horse was nowhere to be found.

Then they began to dig. Sixty thousand hands dug into the earth — deep, and deeper. They went down beneath the earth — and wherever they dug, a great hollow was made.

That hollow became so vast that later it became the ocean — the same ocean we call Sagara today.

Digging and digging, they reached the nether world. And there — they saw the horse.

Pause and think — Sixty thousand sons dug up the earth — and the hollow they dug was filled by the ocean. Can the effect of our deeds sometimes be something we never imagined?

4 · Kapila's Hermitage · · KAPILA'S HERMITAGE

◆ This part is not for younger listeners

In the nether world, where the horse was grazing, there was a hermitage nearby. In it sat the sage Kapila in meditation — calm, grave, eyes closed.

The sixty thousand sons saw the horse — and thought this sage had stolen it. They filled with anger. They called the sage a thief — and rushed at him.

Kapila opened his eyes. His gaze, full of anger, fell upon them — and the sixty thousand sons were burnt to ash there. Heaps of ash remained — and the horse went on grazing as before.

The sage had not stolen the horse. It was Indra who had hidden it — and the sons, without thinking, without asking, had blamed the sage.

Pause and think — The sons called the sage a thief — without asking, without knowing. Do we too sometimes blame someone without knowing? And when that happens, what is the result?

5 · Amshuman's Search · · AMSHUMAN'S SEARCH

In Ayodhya, Sagara waited — but neither the sons nor the horse returned. Then he sent his grandson Amshuman — Asamanja's son.

Amshuman went by the same road — down through the dug-out hollow, to the nether world. There he saw the horse — and beside it, heaps of ash.

Amshuman understood — his sixty thousand uncles were no more. His heart filled. He thought — I shall offer water to their souls — but where was water there? In the nether world there was not a drop.

Then Garuda came — Vishnu's eagle, Amshuman's maternal uncle. He said —

Garuda said: “Amshuman, ordinary water will not liberate them. Only the waters of Ganga — the river of heaven — can purify them and carry them to heaven.”

Amshuman brought the horse back to Ayodhya. Sagara completed the sacrifice. Then Sagara ruled for thirty thousand years — and passed away without bringing Ganga down to earth.

Pause and think — Amshuman saw the heaps of ash — and did not weep, he kept searching. Garuda showed him the way — but the way was long. In sorrow, is searching for the way itself the greatest work?

6 · The Penance of Two Generations · · THE PENANCE OF TWO GENERATIONS

After Sagara, Amshuman became king. He too did penance to bring Ganga — for years. But Ganga did not come.

Amshuman handed the kingdom to his son Dilipa and passed away. Dilipa too did penance — for years, with full devotion. But Ganga did not come.

Two generations passed — from Sagara to Amshuman, from Amshuman to Dilipa. The ash of the sixty thousand sons still lay in the nether world — and Ganga still flowed in heaven.

Then Dilipa had a son — Bhagiratha.

Pause and think — Two generations did penance and failed — yet the third generation began penance again. Is trying again after failure foolishness — or courage?

7 · Bhagiratha's Penance · · BHAGIRATHA'S PENANCE

Bhagiratha too began penance — hard, long, without stopping. He gave up food and drink, fixed his mind, and held only one wish — may Ganga come down to earth.

At last Brahma appeared — the creator, four-faced, in white robes. He said —

Brahma said: “Bhagiratha, I am pleased. Ganga shall come down to earth — but listen, her force will be so fierce that the earth will not be able to bear it. Only Shiva can hold her. First, please Shiva.”

Bhagiratha began penance to Shiva — for one year, standing on the tip of his big toe.

Pause and think — Brahma gave the boon — but along with it he also told him the condition. Is receiving a boon enough — or must one also know the way to receive it?

8 · Ganga in Shiva's Locks · · GANGA IN SHIVA'S LOCKS

A year passed. Shiva was pleased — and said, “I shall hold Ganga.”

Ganga descended from heaven — with great pride. She thought — I shall sweep even Shiva away to the nether world!

But Shiva saw her pride. As soon as Ganga came, Shiva caught her in his matted locks. Ganga was trapped in the locks — she could not escape.

Bhagiratha pleased Shiva once again. Then Shiva released Ganga drop by drop — and Ganga fell into Bindu lake.

Pause and think — Ganga came with pride — and was caught in Shiva's locks. Does pride always block the way — and humility open it?

9 · Seven Streams · · SEVEN STREAMS

From Bindu lake, Ganga flowed in seven streams — three to the east: Hladini, Pavani, Nalini; three to the west: Suchakshu, Sita, Sindhu; and the seventh stream — that one followed Bhagiratha.

Bhagiratha rode ahead in a divine chariot — and Ganga flowed behind him. Apsaras and creatures of the water followed joyfully with them.

Wherever Ganga flowed, the land became holy. People came to the banks to look — the river of heaven was flowing on earth!

Pause and think — Ganga flowed in seven streams — but only the seventh followed Bhagiratha. Does a river too need someone to show it the way — or does it know the way itself?

10 · Jahnavi · · JAHNAVI

On the way, Ganga passed the sacrifice ground of the sage Jahnu — and the flood drowned his sacrifice ground.

Jahnu grew angry — and he drank Ganga up! The whole river — in a single draught.

The gods and sages came — they prayed to Jahnu — “Release Ganga — she is going behind Bhagiratha, for the liberation of sixty thousand sons.”

Jahnu let Ganga out through his ear. Since then Ganga has had another name — Jahnavi — the daughter of Jahnu.

Pause and think — Jahnu drank Ganga up — then let her go. Is a deed done in anger always wrong — or can it sometimes be set right?

11 · The Ocean Is Filled · · THE OCEAN IS FILLED

Ganga flowed on — and reached the ocean. The same ocean — which the sixty thousand sons had dug. Ganga's waters filled it — and the ocean was full.

Then Ganga went down to the nether world — where the heaps of ash lay. Ganga's waters flowed over them — and the souls of the sixty thousand sons, purified, went to heaven.

Brahma gave Ganga another name — Bhagirathi — the daughter of Bhagiratha. Because it was through Bhagiratha's penance that she came down to earth.

And that ocean — which Sagara's sons had dug and Ganga had filled — was named Sagara — after Sagara.

Vishwamitra said — “Rama, this is the story of Ganga's descent — the penance of three generations, the unshaken will of one king, and a river that came down from heaven and made the earth holy.”

The penance of three generations —
and Ganga came down from heaven to earth.

Pause and think — Sagara began the sacrifice, Amshuman did the searching, Dilipa did penance — but Ganga came through Bhagiratha's penance. Is any great work the work of one man alone — or of many generations?

Bigger Thoughts · · FOR LISTENERS

Listening to this story, some questions rise in the mind — ask them of your listeners, and hear their answers:

1. Sagara banished Asamanja from the city — was that right? Should a father punish his own son?

2. The sixty thousand sons called the sage a thief — without asking. Is it right to blame someone without knowing?

3. The penance of Amshuman and Dilipa did not succeed — yet Bhagiratha did penance. Is trying again after failure foolishness — or courage?

4. Ganga came with pride — and was caught in Shiva's locks. Does pride always block the way?

5. Jahnu drank Ganga up — then let her go. Is setting a mistake right as great a work as not making the mistake?

6. Ganga was named Bhagirathi — after Bhagiratha. Is it right for a river to be named after a man — or does a river belong to everyone?

Where This Story Comes From · · SOURCES AND OTHER TELLINGS

The Main Source

The main story of this book is from the Ramayana, Bala Kanda, sargas 38–44 — as Vishwamitra tells it to Rama. Sarga 38: Sagara, his two wives, Asamanja's banishment, the horse sacrifice and Indra taking the horse; sarga 39: the sixty thousand sons digging and being burnt to ash at Kapila's hermitage; sargas 40–41: Amshuman's search, Garuda's counsel, the completion of the sacrifice, Sagara's thirty thousand years of rule and his passing, and the penance of Amshuman and Dilipa; sarga 42: Bhagiratha's penance and Brahma's boon; sarga 43: a year of penance to Shiva, Ganga caught in the locks, released drop by drop, the seven streams, Jahnu drinking Ganga and releasing her, the purification of the ash and the name Bhagirathi.

Why Did Indra Take the Horse

Valmiki says Indra took the horse — the sarga gives no long reason for it. Later tellings say Indra feared Sagara's sacrifice would make him too powerful. That reason belongs to the later tellings, not to Valmiki's sarga — which is why the main story tells only that the horse was taken.

Who Was Kapila

In Valmiki, Kapila is a great sage — sitting in meditation in the nether world. Later tradition also calls him an incarnation of Vishnu, and links him with Kapila of the Sankhya philosophy. In this book he is kept as Valmiki has him — a calm sage sitting in meditation.

The Sound 'Hum'

Some later tellings say Kapila uttered 'Hum' — and the sons turned to ash. In Valmiki it is said that they were burnt by Kapila's angry gaze. The main story keeps Valmiki's telling; the 'Hum' is mentioned only in this note.

The Place of Bhagiratha's Penance

In Valmiki's sarga 42 the place of Bhagiratha's penance is not named — only that he did severe penance. Later tellings name his place of penance as Gokarna. That name belongs to the later tellings — which is why no place is given in the main story.

The Names Bhagirathi and Jahnavi

Ganga received two names from this story — Bhagirathi, because she came down to earth through Bhagiratha's penance (Brahma gave this name), and Jahnavi, because the sage Jahnu let her out through his ear — so she was called the daughter of Jahnu.

The End · · THE END

Here the story of Sagara and Bhagiratha pauses — but Rama's journey goes on. Rising from the banks of the Ganga, Vishwamitra, Rama and Lakshmana walked on toward Mithila — and on the way they had yet another story to hear — of the churning of the ocean, as Valmiki told it — and of Diti's sons, who became the gods of the wind.

That story is in the next book — The Churning of the Ocean — Valmiki's Telling.

— The End —
